i.t: The Qur’an confirms the message of the earlier testaments — the message of Moses and the Messiah, peace be upon them
i.s: One message, one purpose — completed across three testaments
i.x: The Qur’an is the Last Testament: it describes itself as confirming the messages of the messengers who came before it, in a journey of faith that stretches back to the beginning of creation.

i.t: If you believe in the Creator of the universe… read His message to you
i.x: For as long as human beings have lived on this earth, they have asked existential questions they struggle to answer: How did I come to be? Why am I here? What becomes of me after death? Read the answers in “The Last Testament.”

i.t: How does the Last Testament speak of the figures of the earlier testaments?
i.x: The same prophets — with details that may surprise you. Tap any card to read the verse.

i.t: The Torah — as the Qur’an describes it
i.x: (the Torah) How the Qur’an described the Torah — al-Mā’idah 5:44 The context here is a judgement: the Qur’an reminds the Jews that they have the Torah, which contains the judgement of God, and describes it as containing “guidance and light” — a description given at a time when it was a living legal reference that people turned to for judgement.

i.t: The Gospel — as the Qur’an describes it
i.x: (the Gospel) How the Qur’an described the Gospel — al-Mā’idah 5:46 The Gospel is described here with the same words as the Torah (“guidance and light”), with the addition that it came confirming what preceded it — the first appearance of the idea of “successive confirmation” on which the Qur’an later builds its description of itself.

i.t: The Qur’an — as it describes itself
i.x: (the Qur’an) How the Qur’an described itself — al-Aḥqāf 46:30 This description comes from a group of jinn who listened to the Qur’an, not from the Prophet ﷺ himself — a testimony from an outside party, recorded within the Qur’anic text itself.

i.t: Abraham — the intimate friend of God, forefather of the messengers
i.x: Father of the prophets, and forefather of the messengers of all three testaments From his descendants came Moses, Jesus and Muhammad ﷺ — so the bearers of all three messages trace their lineage to him. The Qur’an calls him “the intimate friend of God” (Khalīl Allāh), a title given to no other prophet. The verse does not stop at calling Abraham “the intimate friend of God” — a title given to no other prophet — it makes following his “way” (his path of pure monotheism) the best religion. He is the very forefather to whom Moses, Jesus and Muhammad ﷺ trace their lineage. Of his descendants, or following his path — according to Sūrat al-An‘ām 6:83–86: Isaac Jacob Noah David Solomon Job Joseph Moses Aaron Zechariah John Jesus Elias Ishmael Elisha Jonah Lot

i.t: Ishmael, Isaac and Jacob — the continuation of prophethood
i.x: Abraham’s sons and grandson — and Jacob is “Israel” himself Ishmael helped his father Abraham build the Kaaba, and Isaac and Jacob carried the line of prophethood after him. Jacob is the one known as “Israel,” and his twelve sons are “the Tribes” (al-Asbāṭ). One verse brings all four together: on his deathbed Jacob asks his sons what they will worship, and they answer with pure monotheism — the God of their fathers Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac. Even the word “Muslims” here means those who submit to God alone, not yet the name of a particular religion.

i.t: Moses — the one to whom God spoke
i.x: The person named most often in the Noble Qur’an His name, Mūsā, appears explicitly about 136 times — more than any other person. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ himself is named explicitly only 4 times, even though the Qur’an addresses him directly, without naming him, in thousands of verses. This verse is the origin of Moses’ title “Kalīm Allāh” (the one to whom God spoke): he was chosen by God’s “messages” and by His “words” together. The “tablets” mentioned here are the same ones Jews and Christians know as the Ten Commandments — a direct Qur’anic acknowledgement of them as instruction and explanation.

i.t: David — slayer of Goliath and bearer of the Psalms
i.x: God gave him kingship, wisdom and knowledge The brave warrior-prophet who brought victory to the Children of Israel by slaying their enemy, Goliath. God then gave him kingship and wisdom, and taught him what He willed — including certain crafts. The story of David and Goliath is known even outside religious settings — an immediate point of recognition for the reader. Elsewhere (Saba’ 34:10) the Qur’an describes how the mountains and the birds echoed God’s praise with him, and how iron was made soft in his hands.

He understood the speech of birds and ants The wind and the jinn were made subservient to him, and he was taught the language of birds — and his full story with the Queen of Sheba is told in detail in the Qur’an. The first verse to announce that Solomon was taught the language of birds — a prelude to the detailed story of the hoopoe and the Queen of Sheba in the rest of the chapter.

i.t: Mary — chosen above the women of the worlds
i.x: The only woman mentioned by name — chosen above the women of the worlds Of all the women in the Qur’an, Mary alone is mentioned by name (34 times), and a whole chapter bears her name — the angels themselves tell her that God has chosen her above the women of the worlds. A direct address from the angels to Mary — one of the reasons some scholars have studied her exalted rank among the prophets and the righteous.

Born of a virgin, he raised the dead by God’s permission The Qur’an affirms his miraculous birth to the Virgin Mary, and that God worked great miracles through him: healing the blind and the leper, and bringing the dead to life — by God’s permission. Jesus’ miracles here are very close to those recorded in the Gospels — healing the blind and the leper, and raising the dead. The one doctrinal difference is that the Qur’an repeats “by permission of God” with each miracle, stressing that the power belongs to God alone.

i.t: Muhammad ﷺ — the seal of the prophets
i.x: The seal of the prophets, and a mercy to the worlds The Qur’an calls him “the seal of the prophets” — the last link in this long chain from Abraham to Jesus — and affirms that his message is not for one particular people but “a mercy to the worlds,” to all. “The seal of the prophets” is the origin of this website’s name, “The Last Testament”: the Qur’an declares itself the close of the chain of prophethood that began with Abraham, while the second verse affirms that the message is not confined to one people or time, but is for all the worlds.

i.t: The Last Testament (the Noble Qur’an) — the seal of the heavenly messages
i.x: God sent Moses, peace be upon him, to the Children of Israel with the Torah — “the Old Testament.” After him He sent Jesus, son of Mary, peace be upon them both, with the Gospel — “the New Testament.” Then came the Last Testament, the Noble Qur’an, brought by Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, as the final message of the prophets. All of these messengers descend from Abraham, the father of the prophets: Moses and Jesus descend from Jacob son of Isaac son of Abraham, and Muhammad descends from Ishmael son of Abraham — they are cousins, all from the line of Abraham, peace and blessings be upon them all.
